<PropertyGroup Condition="'$(TargetFramework)' == 'net8.0'">
  <GenerateDocumentationFile>true</GenerateDocumentationFile>
</PropertyGroup>
```

### 🔴 E2 — `Directory.Build.targets`: Property defaults in `.targets` override project-level values
**File:** `Directory.Build.targets`, lines 6–10

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>
  <Company>Contoso</Company>
  ...
</PropertyGroup>
```

**Problem:** `.targets` is imported **after** the project file. MSBuild uses last-write-wins semantics, so this unconditionally overwrites any value set in a `.csproj`. This is the direct cause of LibB's issue: LibB explicitly sets `TreatWarningsAsErrors=false` (line 13), but this `.targets` file silently stomps it back to `true`.

Property defaults that should be overridable by individual projects belong in `Directory.Build.props` with conditional guards:

**Fix:**
```xml
<!-- In Directory.Build.props -->
<PropertyGroup>
  <TreatWarningsAsErrors Condition="'$(TreatWarningsAsErrors)' == ''">true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>
  <Company Condition="'$(Company)' == ''">Contoso</Company>
  <Authors Condition="'$(Authors)' == ''">Build Team</Authors>
  <Copyright Condition="'$(Copyright)' == ''">Copyright 2024 Contoso</Copyright>
</PropertyGroup>
```

---

### 🔴 E3 — `LibA.csproj`: `DefineConstants` overwrites instead of appending
**File:** `LibA.csproj`, line 14

```xml
<DefineConstants>ENABLE_LOGGING</DefineConstants>
```

**Problem:** This replaces the entire `DefineConstants` list. The SDK-injected defaults (`DEBUG`, `TRACE` for Debug configuration) are silently destroyed. Any `#if DEBUG` or `#if TRACE` checks in code will always evaluate to `false` in Debug builds.

**Fix:**
```xml
<DefineConstants>$(DefineConstants);ENABLE_LOGGING</DefineConstants>
```

---

### 🔴 E4 — `LibA.csproj`: Unquoted condition value
**File:** `LibA.csproj`, line 13

```xml
<PropertyGroup Condition="$(Configuration) == Debug">
```

**Problem:** The condition is unquoted. If `$(Configuration)` is empty (e.g., during evaluation or restore), this evaluates as ` == Debug` which is a malformed expression that can cause an MSBuild evaluation error. Additionally, values with spaces would break parsing.

**Fix:**
```xml
<PropertyGroup Condition="'$(Configuration)' == 'Debug'">
```

### 🔴 E5 — `LibA.csproj`: Publish-on-build target re-invokes the same project, causing double-build and potential file race
**File:** `LibA.csproj`, lines 43–45

```xml
<Target Name="PublishOnBuild" AfterTargets="Build">
  <MSBuild Projects="$(MSBuildProjectFullPath)" Targets="Publish" Properties="_IsPublishing=true" />
</Target>
```

**Problem:** This forks a **second MSBuild evaluation** of the same project file with different global properties (`_IsPublishing=true`). MSBuild treats this as a distinct project instance, so it builds the project again from scratch. The two instances race to write the same output files (`bin/`, `obj/`), which can cause intermittent file-in-use errors or corrupted outputs. This also doubles the build time for LibA (and transitively delays LibB).

**Fix:** Use `DependsOnTargets` to run publish logic in the same project instance, or remove this target and use `dotnet publish` explicitly in CI.

### 🔴 E6 — `BrokenOrder.fsproj`: F# compile order is wrong — will cause build failure
**File:** `fsharp/BrokenOrder/BrokenOrder.fsproj`, lines 7–9

```xml
<Compile Include="Services.fs" />   <!-- Uses Domain types -->
<Compile Include="Domain.fs" />     <!-- Defines Domain types -->
<Compile Include="Program.fs" />
```

**Problem:** F# is order-dependent — files can only reference types/modules defined in files listed *above* them. `Services.fs` opens `BrokenOrder.Domain` (defined in `Domain.fs`), but `Domain.fs` is listed *after* `Services.fs`. This will produce a compilation error: `FS0039: The namespace or module 'BrokenOrder.Domain' is not defined`.

Compare with the working `OrderService.fsproj` which has the correct order: `Domain.fs` → `Services.fs` → `Program.fs`.

**Fix:**
```xml
<Compile Include="Domain.fs" />
<Compile Include="Services.fs" />
<Compile Include="Program.fs" />
```

### 🟡 W1 — `Directory.Build.props`: Analyzer package leaks to downstream consumers
**File:** `Directory.Build.props`, lines 16–18

```xml
<PackageReference Include="StyleCop.Analyzers" Version="1.2.0-beta.556" />
```

**Problem:** Without `PrivateAssets="all"`, this analyzer package flows transitively to any NuGet consumer of LibA or LibB. Downstream projects would unexpectedly inherit StyleCop rules and potentially fail builds due to style violations they never opted into.

**Fix:**
```xml
<PackageReference Include="StyleCop.Analyzers" Version="1.2.0-beta.556">
  <PrivateAssets>all</PrivateAssets>
  <IncludeAssets>runtime; build; native; contentfiles; analyzers</IncludeAssets>
</PackageReference>
```

### 🟡 W2 — `LibA.csproj`: Hardcoded Windows-absolute `OutputPath`
**File:** `LibA.csproj`, line 7 / `LibB.csproj`, line 7

```xml
<OutputPath>C:\builds\output\LibA</OutputPath>
<OutputPath>C:\builds\output\LibB</OutputPath>
```

**Problem:** These are Windows-absolute paths (`C:\…`). On Linux/macOS CI agents, these paths are meaningless — MSBuild will interpret `C:` as a relative directory name, producing bizarre output locations like `./C:/builds/output/LibA/`. This also prevents developers from building locally without this exact directory structure. Hardcoded paths are fragile and non-portable.

**Fix:** Use a relative path or a configurable property:
```xml
<OutputPath>$(MSBuildThisFileDirectory)..\artifacts\LibA\</OutputPath>
```

### 🟡 W3 — `LibA.csproj`: Bare `<Reference>` with HintPath to `packages\` folder (legacy pattern)
**File:** `LibA.csproj`, lines 27–29

```xml
<Reference Include="Newtonsoft.Json">
  <HintPath>..\packages\Newtonsoft.Json.13.0.3\lib\net6.0\Newtonsoft.Json.dll</HintPath>
</Reference>
```

**Problem:** This is the legacy `packages.config` pattern of referencing NuGet packages. In an SDK-style project, this bypasses NuGet's dependency resolution entirely — the package won't be restored by `dotnet restore`, the TFM-matching is wrong (referencing `net6.0` lib in a `net8.0` project), and transitive dependencies won't be pulled in. This assembly will likely not be found at build time.

**Fix:** Replace with a `PackageReference`:
```xml
<PackageReference Include="Newtonsoft.Json" Version="13.0.3" />
```

---

### 🟡 W4 — `LibA.csproj`: Redundant `<Compile Include>` causes CS2002 duplicate-file warning
**File:** `LibA.csproj`, lines 21–23

```xml
<Compile Include="Class1.cs" />
<Compile Update="Class1.cs" AutoGen="true" />
```

**Problem:** The SDK automatically glob-includes all `*.cs` files. The explicit `<Compile Include="Class1.cs" />` adds the file a second time, which produces a `CS2002` duplicate source file warning. The `Update` on the next line should be used alone — `Update` modifies metadata on an existing item without re-adding it.

**Fix:** Remove the `Include` line, keep only `Update`:
```xml
<ItemGroup>
  <Compile Update="Class1.cs" AutoGen="true" />
</ItemGroup>
```

### 🟡 W5 — `LibA.csproj`: Custom target `PrintVersion` missing `Inputs`/`Outputs`
**File:** `LibA.csproj`, lines 32–34

```xml
<Target Name="PrintVersion" BeforeTargets="Build">
  <Exec Command="echo Building version 1.0.0" />
</Target>
```

**Problem:** Without `Inputs`/`Outputs` attributes, this target runs on every single build, even no-op incremental builds. This breaks incrementality and slows the edit-compile-debug cycle. Additionally, the version `1.0.0` is hardcoded in the `Exec` command rather than using `$(Version)` or `$(AssemblyVersion)`.

**Fix:** Either add `Inputs`/`Outputs` to make it incremental, or if it's truly informational, accept the cost. At minimum use the property:
```xml
<Exec Command="echo Building version $(Version)" />
```
